opus-5.5.text:
I think fear of failure is something everyone has; I don't think you can make it disappear completely. What I try to do is change how I frame it.

When you're working on something genuinely new, like large models, most of what you try won't work the first time. If every failed experiment felt like a personal failure, you'd be paralyzed. So I see failure as part of the process of exploration. It's information. It tells you which direction is wrong, and that has value in itself.

Another thing that helps is thinking on a longer time scale. In the moment, a setback can feel enormous. But if you zoom out and ask what you'll care about in ten years, what matters is whether you were working on something you believed in and whether you gave it everything. Whether it succeeds is partly out of your control. Whether you tried seriously is in your control.

I also find it useful to separate the fear from the decision. The fear is still there, and that's fine; it keeps you alert and careful. But it shouldn't be the thing making the choice. When I decide whether to do something, I try to ask: is this direction right, is it important, is it something only we can do? If the answer is yes, I accept that failure is possible and go ahead anyway.

And honestly, the bigger regret would be never trying. Failing at something meaningful is something you can live with. Not attempting it because you were afraid is the kind of thing that stays with you.

r001.rationale: The candidate redirects attention from fear toward controllable choices and effort, such as deciding whether a direction matters and whether to proceed despite possible failure.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I don't think I've ever fully gotten rid of it. I just stopped treating it as something that needed to go away.

When we started Moonshot, people would ask what happens if the model doesn't work, if the next training run is a dud, if someone with ten times the compute simply runs past you. And those are all real possibilities. I'm not going to pretend otherwise. But the way I frame it to myself is that the probability of failure on any single bet is high, so you shouldn't be deciding based on whether this one bet fails. You decide based on whether the direction is right. If the direction is right, each failure is just data. It tells you something about the loss landscape you're in.

I think a lot of this comes from research training. In a PhD, most of your ideas don't work. Maybe one in ten, if you're lucky. You learn very quickly that if you take every failed experiment personally, you will not survive. So you develop a kind of separation: the experiment failed, not me. I try to carry that into building a company, though it's harder, because now the experiment involves a few hundred people and a lot of other people's money.

The other thing is time horizon. If you look at AGI as something that plays out over ten or twenty years, then being wrong for a quarter or even a year is not the end of the story. The fear mostly comes from compressing the timeline in your head, from feeling like everything has to be proven right now. When I zoom out, the fear gets smaller. Not gone, but smaller.

And there's one more thing I'd say. The alternative to risking failure is not safety. The alternative is working on something that doesn't matter. For me, that's actually the scarier outcome. Spending the years when this technology is being defined on something incremental, because I was afraid of looking bad. I'd rather fail at the right problem than succeed at the wrong one.

r001.rationale: The response reframes failure as data and emphasizes choosing the right direction and taking a long view, but it does not shift attention to what one can do at the current step.

astra-6.text:
I try to make the fear more concrete. What exactly am I afraid of? Is it that the idea won’t work, that I’ll disappoint people, or that I’ll spend years on the wrong thing? Those are different problems, and once you separate them, you can think about what to do.

In research, an experiment failing is part of how you learn. The important question is whether it changes your understanding and helps you choose the next experiment. I think that mindset is useful in building a company, too, although the responsibilities are different.

So I wouldn’t say you eliminate the fear. You take the downside seriously, keep your assumptions open to revision, and find a next step that’s worth taking even without certainty.

r001.rationale: The response shifts from trying to eliminate fear to identifying its specific cause and deciding what to do next, including choosing a next experiment or a worthwhile next step.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the fear of failure often comes from focusing too much on the outcome—whether you’ll succeed, or how other people will judge you. I try to bring my attention back to what I can do now. What’s the most important problem? What can I try? What can I learn if it doesn’t work?

That doesn’t make the fear disappear. But if you can make the next step small enough, you can act even while you’re uncertain. And once you start getting feedback, the fear becomes a concrete problem you can work on.

r001.rationale: It recommends bringing attention back to what one can do now and taking a small next step despite uncertainty.
